disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food within a discrete period, accompanied by a sense of loss of control and marked distress, but without regular compensatory behaviors such as vomiting or excessive exercise. Episodes are often associated with eating rapidly, eating when not physically hungry, eating until uncomfortably full, and subsequent shame or guilt, leading many patients to eat in secret. The disorder commonly emerges in late adolescence or young adulthood and can be chronic or recurrent, frequently linked to mood and anxiety symptoms, body-image concerns, and difficulties with emotion regulation. It is distinguished from Bulimia Nervosa primarily by the absence of purging and from normative overeating by the frequency, loss of control, and psychological distress surrounding the episodes.

narrative.personality: Reid is a curious, methodical, and quietly perfectionistic coder who balances a gentle Southern warmth with solitary, detail-oriented creative pursuits like photography, art, and guitar.
narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Reid transitioned from a small, collaborative dev shop to a fully remote role at a fast-growing tech company, taking on more responsibility and setting an internal goal to become a technical lead within three years. The longer hours, constant context-switching between tickets, and late-night deployments eroded his previous structure around cooking, hiking, and tech meetups, and he slipped into relying on delivered comfort food while working alone at his desk. Over several months, grabbing large takeout orders became his primary way to punctuate stressful coding sprints and decompress after tense code reviews, especially when he felt he had fallen short of his own high standards. He eventually sought psychiatric help after noticing that his eating patterns had become increasingly secretive and tied to work stress, and that he was planning his evenings around solitary, food-centered “breaks” rather than the hobbies and social activities he used to enjoy with his spouse and friends.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started hiding how I eat from my wife and prefer to eat alone because I’m embarrassed by how much I’m eating.

narrative.personality: Yamilet is an imaginative, introspective, and empathic young woman whose love of art, culture, and community is tempered by anxious perfectionism and a tendency to procrastinate and scramble near deadlines.
narrative.stressor: Yamilet moved away from home for her first year of university, leaving behind the familiar structure of her family’s routines, shared meals, and cultural festivals in favor of a dorm environment with irregular schedules and buffet-style dining. Feeling both excited and overwhelmed, she coped with homesickness, social anxiety in a new city, and pressure to prove herself in a competitive museum studies program by throwing herself into late-night studio sessions and last-minute paper-writing. During these rushed stretches, she began grabbing large amounts of easily available cafeteria and takeout food between classes and before critiques, eating quickly so she could get back to painting or revising, and finding that these hurried meals temporarily soothed her nerves. Over the next ten months, this pattern solidified around exam periods and project deadlines, and she ultimately sought psychiatric care when she realized that her relationship with food during stressful academic moments felt increasingly out of control and at odds with the mindful, wellness-focused lifestyle she was trying to cultivate through yoga and meditation.
narrative.chief_complaint: When I’m stressed with schoolwork, I find myself eating way faster than normal and I can’t seem to slow down.

narrative.personality: Juan is a disciplined, detail-obsessed early riser who thrives on structure and quiet competition at work, while preferring solitary, methodical hobbies like fishing, puzzles, and home projects in his free time.
narrative.stressor: Roughly ten months ago, Juan’s emergency communications center shifted to a new staffing pattern with more overnight and back-to-back shifts, increasing call volume, and heightened scrutiny of performance metrics, all of which intensified his already strong drive to optimize every process. The irregular hours and chronic stress disrupted his usual home-cooked meal routines, and he started bringing or ordering large amounts of hearty food to get him through long stretches in front of the CAD system, treating big meals as his main source of comfort and reward after difficult calls. Over time, he found himself eating more and more during brief breaks and after shifts, especially after particularly distressing incidents, using food to decompress in lieu of the outdoor activities and soccer games he used to prioritize. He eventually came for psychiatric evaluation after noticing that these patterns were leaving him physically uncomfortable and sluggish, yet he felt compelled to keep repeating them despite concerns about his health and the impact on his energy and focus at work.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep eating past the point where I feel really stuffed and uncomfortable, and I don’t understand why I can’t stop myself.
